Italian Renaissance · Quattrocento / Cinquecento

Leonardo da Vinci

1452 – 1519

Illegitimate son of a Tuscan notary, apprenticed in Verrocchio’s Florentine bottega, who across courts in Milan, Florence, Rome, and France filled 7,000+ notebook pages with painting, anatomy, engineering, hydraulics, optics, and flight – leaving only about 15 finished paintings, but redefining what a single mind could attempt.

Born
Anchiano, near Vinci
Republic of Florence
Died
Clos Lucé, Amboise, France
May 2, 1519
Nationality
Florentine (Italian)
Known for
Last Supper, Mona Lisa, Vitruvian Man, anatomical & engineering notebooks

A Life in Five Eras

Leonardo lived 67 years across four Italian courts and the French royal court, from the village of Anchiano below the hill town of Vinci to the manor of Clos Lucé at Amboise. He left around 15 finished paintings – and roughly 7,000 surviving notebook pages on painting, anatomy, engineering, hydraulics, optics, geology, and flight.

Verrocchio & Leonardo, Baptism of Christ, c. 1472–75 (Uffizi). The angel on the left is the young Leonardo’s contribution to his master’s panel.

Vinci & the Florentine Apprenticeship

1452 – 1482

Born April 15, 1452 in the village of Anchiano, below the small Tuscan hill town of Vinci. He was the illegitimate son of Ser Piero da Vinci, a twenty-five-year-old notary, and Caterina, a young peasant woman the family quickly married off to a local laborer. Illegitimacy barred Leonardo from the universities and the notary’s guild that his father practiced – an exclusion that, perversely, freed him to learn by direct observation rather than by Latin textbook. He spent his earliest years between his mother’s household and his grandfather Antonio’s farm.

Around 1466 his father moved him to Florence and apprenticed him to Andrea del Verrocchio, whose bottega was the leading workshop of the city. There Leonardo trained alongside Sandro Botticelli, Pietro Perugino, and Domenico Ghirlandaio, learning oil painting, bronze casting, anatomy from dissected animals, and engineering from Verrocchio’s commissions on the dome of the Florence cathedral. Vasari records that the master, on seeing the angel his young apprentice had painted in the Baptism of Christ, set down his brush and resolved never to paint again.

“He would often pass the entire day visualizing, and never put hand to pencil. And when he had brought the work to that perfection which his genius required, he would then with the greatest reluctance lay it aside as unfinished.” – Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists, on Leonardo’s working method, 1550
Key Moment 1481: the monks of San Donato a Scopeto commission an altarpiece, the Adoration of the Magi. Leonardo begins, sketches a revolutionary composition full of rearing horses and astonished faces, and then in 1482 simply leaves Florence for Milan without finishing it. The unfinished panel becomes the signature of his career: enormous ambition, real innovation, abandoned execution.
Leonardo da Vinci, The Last Supper, 1495–98. Refectory wall, Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan. Painted in experimental oil-on-dry-plaster that began deteriorating within a generation.

Milan & the Sforza Court

1482 – 1499

In 1482, age 30, Leonardo wrote one of the most extraordinary job applications in history: a draft letter to Ludovico Sforza, the de-facto ruler of Milan. Across ten numbered paragraphs he offered “light, sturdy bridges,” methods for draining moats, “covered chariots, safe and unattackable” (proto-tanks), bombards, mortars, ships, secret tunnels, and architecture. Only the eleventh and final paragraph mentioned, almost as an afterthought: “I can also execute sculpture in marble, bronze, and clay; likewise in painting, whatever may be done.” He got the job.

For seventeen years in Milan he was court engineer, festival designer, military consultant, anatomist, and only secondarily a painter. He worked on a vast clay model for a 24-foot bronze equestrian statue of Ludovico’s father (the bronze was diverted to cannon when the French invaded; the clay horse was destroyed by Gascon archers using it for target practice). He painted the Virgin of the Rocks, the Lady with an Ermine (Ludovico’s mistress Cecilia Gallerani), and across 1495–98 the Last Supper on the wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie. He filled notebook after notebook with anatomy, hydraulics, the geometry of Luca Pacioli’s De divina proportione, and around 1490 the Vitruvian Man.

“Most illustrious Lord, having now sufficiently considered the specimens of all those who proclaim themselves skilled contrivers of instruments of war… I will endeavor, without prejudice to anyone else, to explain myself to your Excellency, showing your Lordship my secret.” – Leonardo, draft letter to Ludovico Sforza, c. 1482, Codex Atlanticus
Key Moment October 1499: French armies under Louis XII enter Milan; Ludovico flees, is captured, and dies in a French prison. Leonardo’s clay horse is shot to pieces by French archers. His seventeen-year court career ends overnight, and he leaves the city carrying notebooks, the unfinished Battle of Anghiari cartoons yet to come, and the certainty that paintings on walls do not survive war.
Leonardo da Vinci, Mona Lisa (La Gioconda), begun c. 1503, Florence. Carried with Leonardo to France; never delivered to her merchant husband Francesco del Giocondo.

Wandering Italy, Borgia, and the Mona Lisa

1500 – 1513

Leonardo crossed back to Florence in 1500, age 48, and found the city different. Botticelli was burning his own paintings under Savonarola’s influence; a younger genius named Michelangelo was carving the David from a slab of Carrara marble. The Signoria commissioned both artists to paint rival battle frescoes in the new Palazzo Vecchio council hall – Michelangelo’s Battle of Cascina and Leonardo’s Battle of Anghiari. Leonardo’s experimental wax-medium paints failed to set; the work was abandoned and later painted over.

From summer 1502 through early 1503 Leonardo served as chief military engineer to Cesare Borgia during the Romagna campaign, drawing extraordinary bird’s-eye-view fortress maps and consulting (alongside the Florentine secretary Niccolò Machiavelli) on a doomed scheme to divert the Arno River around Pisa. By 1503 he was back in Florence beginning the portrait of Lisa Gherardini, wife of the silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo – the Mona Lisa, which he would carry with him for the next 16 years and never deliver. He never stopped working on it.

“The painter is lord of all manner of people and of all things. If the painter wishes to see beauties that charm him, it lies in his power to create them; and if he wishes to see monstrosities that are frightful, comical, or truly pitiable, he is lord and god thereof.” – Leonardo, Trattato della Pittura (Treatise on Painting), c. 1500
Key Moment June 1502: Leonardo joins Cesare Borgia’s entourage as senior military engineer. Over the next eight months he produces some of the most accurate maps of the era. He also begins to record, with strange clinical detachment, the violence Borgia uses to consolidate the Romagna – including the December 1502 massacre at Senigallia, in which Machiavelli was also present.
Leonardo da Vinci, anatomical study of the human skull, c. 1489 (Royal Collection, Windsor). One of more than 200 surviving anatomy sheets – notebooks of dissection that anticipated modern systematic anatomy by a century.

Rome & the Vatican Years

1513 – 1516

In September 1513, with the Medici newly returned to power and Giovanni de’ Medici elected as Pope Leo X, Leonardo moved to Rome under the patronage of the pope’s younger brother Giuliano. He was given rooms in the Belvedere at the Vatican, a stipend, and a workshop. He was also 61 years old, and Rome belonged now to Raphael (in his thirties, painting the Stanze) and to Michelangelo (finishing the Sistine ceiling, then sketching its altar wall). Leonardo, the older master, was edged to the periphery.

He worked in Rome with the young Pavian anatomist Marcantonio della Torre on a planned anatomical treatise; the most extraordinary work of his life as a scientist dates from these years – thirty sheets on the heart at Windsor, including the realization that the heart is a muscle and that its valves close by hydrodynamic eddies in the outflow chambers (not confirmed by modern medicine until the 1960s). His paintings dwindled to a few works. Vasari hints, and the papal staff complained, that Leonardo seemed more interested in dissecting cadavers and distilling oils than in finishing his commissions. By 1515, Marcantonio was dead of plague at 30; the anatomy project went unfinished.

“This man will never accomplish anything: he thinks of the end before the beginning.” – Pope Leo X, reportedly, on hearing that Leonardo was busy distilling herbs for an experimental varnish instead of beginning a commissioned painting (Vasari, 1550)
Key Moment Winter 1513–14: Leonardo and Marcantonio della Torre dissect a hundred-year-old man whose autopsy reveals narrowed coronary arteries. Leonardo’s sketches of the heart and its valves, and his recognition that the heart is a muscle, constitute the first systematic cardiac anatomy in European medicine. The manuscript sits unread in private collections until the 19th century.
Drawing of the Castle of Amboise, attributed to Leonardo or Francesco Melzi, c. 1518. Just down the Loire from the Cloux (Clos Lucé) manor house where Leonardo lived as guest of King Francis I.

France & Death at Amboise

1516 – 1519

With Giuliano de’ Medici dead and Rome closed to him, Leonardo accepted an invitation from the new young king of France, Francis I, who had just won the battle of Marignano against the Sforza. Late in 1516, age 64, Leonardo crossed the Alps with his pupil Francesco Melzi, his companion Salai, and three paintings he refused to leave behind: the Mona Lisa, the Saint John the Baptist, and the Virgin and Child with Saint Anne. The king housed him at the manor of Cloux (today Clos Lucé), a few hundred yards from the royal château of Amboise, connected (legend holds) by a tunnel.

Francis I gave him the title “First Painter, Engineer, and Architect to the King” and a stipend of 1,000 gold crowns. Leonardo did very little painting in France. His right hand was partly paralyzed (perhaps from a stroke); Melzi did the drawing. Leonardo organized his decades of notebooks for posthumous publication that never quite happened. He designed mechanical lions for court festivities, sketched fluid dynamics, and on April 23, 1519, made out his will leaving his notebooks to Melzi and his vineyard near Milan to Salai. He died on May 2, 1519. Vasari reports, almost certainly inventing, that King Francis I held him as he died.

“As a well-spent day brings happy sleep, so a life well used brings happy death.” – Leonardo, notebook, undated
Key Moment May 2, 1519, Clos Lucé, Amboise: Leonardo dies, age 67. Of his roughly 15 finished paintings, the Mona Lisa stays in France and enters the royal collection; it hangs in the Louvre today. Of his approximately 13,000 notebook pages, Melzi inherits and protects them; after Melzi’s death in 1570 his heirs scatter them, and only about 7,000 pages survive into the present. The astonishing scope of his anatomical and engineering work will not be fully known to the public for another three hundred years.

In His Own Words & Check for Understanding

Leonardo wrote, in mirror-handed Italian, across roughly 13,000 notebook pages. About 7,000 survive. The four passages below are central. Read each one closely; the prompt at the bottom of each card asks the kind of analytical question a teacher would put to a class or you might write about on an essay exam.

Draft letter from Leonardo to Ludovico Sforza
c. 1482 · the Milan job application, Codex Atlanticus
Most illustrious Lord, having now sufficiently considered the specimens of all those who proclaim themselves skilled contrivers of instruments of war... I shall endeavor, without prejudice to anyone else, to explain myself to your Excellency, showing your Lordship my secret, and then offering them to your best pleasure and approbation to work with effect at opportune moments on all those things which, in part, shall be briefly noted below. 1. I have plans for very light, strong and easily portable bridges with which to pursue and... defeat the enemy... 2. I know how, in the course of the siege of a terrain, to remove water from the moats... 3. I have plans for making cannon, very convenient and easy to transport... 9. Where the use of cannon is impracticable, I will assemble catapults, mangonels, trabocchi, and other instruments of wonderful efficacy not in general use... 10. In time of peace I believe I can give perfect satisfaction and to the equal of any other in architecture and the composition of buildings public and private... Item: I can carry out sculpture in marble, bronze, or clay, and also I can do in painting whatever may be done, as well as any other, be he whom he may.
Read closely Across the first nine numbered paragraphs Leonardo offers himself to Ludovico Sforza as a military engineer. Painting is mentioned only in the eleventh, almost as a postscript. Why would a 30-year-old painter trained in Verrocchio’s bottega sell himself this way? What does the order of the items tell you about what the courts of late-Quattrocento Italy valued, and where Leonardo positioned himself among the available patronage markets?
Notebook entry on perpetual motion
c. 1494 · Codex Forster II
O speculators about perpetual motion, how many vain chimeras have you created in the like quest? Go and take your place with the seekers after gold! Among the superfluous and impossible delusions of man is the search for continual motion, called by some the perpetual wheel... For if it were possible that a wheel could move itself perpetually, then we should expect that nature, who is much more powerful than ourselves and who never errs in her operations, would have given us such an instrument; but she has not. And note that no inanimate thing can move of itself; therefore if it moves, it is moved by some unequal weight, and when the weight is balanced the motion will cease.
Read closely Leonardo is, in 1494, dismissing perpetual motion machines. The principle he reaches by observation – that no isolated mechanical system can move itself without an external imbalance – is essentially the first law of thermodynamics, three centuries before Carnot and Joule formalized it. Identify the line of reasoning he uses. What role does “nature” (and her observed behavior) play as a check on speculation? How is this different from a medieval scholastic argument that would invoke logic or scripture?
Leonardo da Vinci, notebook page on fetal anatomy with mirror-writing annotations, c. 1511 (Royal Collection, Windsor, RCIN 919102). Leonardo’s notebooks were written right-to-left in a mirror script that may have been a privacy strategy, a left-handed convenience, or both.
Notebook on the anatomy of the heart
c. 1513 · Anatomical Manuscript B, Royal Collection Windsor
The heart of itself is not the beginning of life; but is a vessel made of dense muscle, vivified and nourished by an artery and a vein as are the other muscles... It is the motion of the heart which is the cause of the motion of the blood... The motion of the blood through the heart is not effected by the diaphragm, but by the muscles of the heart itself. And although these muscles seem to be weaker than other muscles of the body, nevertheless they exhibit such force that no other muscle equals them in the strength of their motion.
Read closely For a thousand years, European medicine following Galen had taught that the heart was a furnace warming the blood, not a muscle pumping it. Leonardo here states directly that the heart is a muscle and that it moves the blood by its own contraction. He has reached this conclusion through dissection (around 30 human cadavers across his career) and through a hydraulic model of valve closure he built from glass. Why is the claim “the heart is a muscle” a more important breakthrough than it sounds – what other long-running medical orthodoxies does it dismantle? And why did European medicine not absorb this insight in 1513?
Notebook on the flight of birds
c. 1505 · Codex on the Flight of Birds, Biblioteca Reale Turin
A bird is an instrument working according to mathematical law, which instrument it is within the capacity of man to reproduce with all its movements, but not with a corresponding degree of strength... The science of mechanics is the most noble and the most useful above all others, since by means of it all animated bodies which have movement perform all their actions; and the origin of these movements is at the center of their gravity, which is placed in the middle, with unequal weights on the sides... When the bird in the air finds that the wind which strikes it is greater than the resistance which the bird makes against the wind, the wind drives the bird with itself; but if the resistance of the bird is greater than the impetus of the wind, the bird overcomes the wind and rises against it.
Read closely Leonardo claims that flight is a problem of mechanics: a bird is “an instrument working according to mathematical law.” The Wright brothers would not fly until 1903 – four centuries after this notebook page – and the achievement would depend not on muscle-powered flapping (which Leonardo’s ornithopter designs assumed) but on fixed wings, a light internal-combustion engine, and an understanding of three-axis control. Which parts of Leonardo’s framing are correct? Which assumption (that humans could supply the “corresponding degree of strength” via mechanical advantage) was the one that kept human flight impossible until the 20th century?
